content.title: What Happened at Justin Bieber’s Coachella 2026 Performance?
content.text: Everything That Happened During Bieberchella 2026 Photo: Photo by Kevin Mazur/Getty Images for Coachella Friday marked the highly anticipated kickoff to Coachella weekend one, and despite being anchored by Sabrina Carpenter and featuring buzzy performances by Katseye, Dijon, and the xx, the name on everybody’s lips on day one was Justin Bieber. On Saturday night, the Canadian heartthrob finally took the stage for his first headlining performance at the festival, using it as an opportunity to (yet again) reinvent his celebrity with a few close collaborators and a YouTube browser. The show marked something of a comeback for Bieber. Last year, he broke his unofficial hiatus with the release of SWAG and SWAG II, followed by a literal stripped-down performance of “Yukon” at the 2026 Grammys. And though he’s popped up at the festival a handful of times before — first in 2014 as a surprise guest of Chance the Rapper and most recently in 2024 when he joined Tems and Wizkid to perform their remix of “Essence” — the Bieberchella hype was real, evidenced by the swift sellout of Bieber’s merch (made by his brand Skylrk). I, a casual fan, snagged several pieces of SWAG-themed clothing, including a neon-green “STANDING ON BUSINESS” T-shirt. After seeing the set, I’m pleased to report my hundreds of dollars were well spent. If you couldn’t make it to the desert (or if Bieber’s slower acoustic cuts lulled you to sleep), here’s a recap of everything that happened over the course of his 90-minute set. There was a charged excitement in the lead-up to Bieber’s performance, especially heightened considering his performances in the last decade have been hard to come by (his 2022–23 Justice World Tour was cut short early due to complications with Ramsay Hunt syndrome). A woman next to me posed the apt question: “When’s the next time you’re gonna get to see Justin Bieber, you know?” Everyone seemed to be on the same page, even Julian Casablancas: During the Strokes’ performance earlier in the evening, he screamed “JUSTIN BIEBER!” to massive cheers from the audience. People don’t play about the man! The entire performance dealt in assured simplicity from the 32-year-old. His SWAG era has been radically pared back by pop-star standards, and the set — a minimalist, solitary ode to devotion — drew on those aesthetics. It’s a testament to the power of his new musical direction, trading theatrics for an unpretentious stage design that allowed the music to speak for itself. Quiet-storm cuts like “ALL I CAN TAKE” and “SPEED DEMON” led the set list, and Bieber seemed to lose himself in ballads like “GO BABY.” He didn’t need backup dancers, fancy visuals, or choreography to put on a good show. His pitch-perfect vocals didn’t hurt. The first part of the set focused solely on cuts from SWAG and SWAG II, taking his laid-back, bedroom R&B in front of a global audience. These are songs that are, in his words, “nice and sultry and sweet.” Rather than building up the audience into hysterics, listening to songs like “BUTTERFLIES” and “ALL THE WAY” felt like drinking an ice-cold glass of water. The vibes got a little worship-music-coded, especially as he moved into renditions of “GLORY VOICE MEMO” and “HALLELUJAH,” but he’s a dad and husband now, with a lot of love in his heart. The sweetness was palpable and felt like a major decompression from the festival’s momentum. (A compliment, btw.) As the performance progressed, Bieber opened up in front of the crowd, eventually shedding his incognito zip-up hoodie and sunglasses in favor of loose movements and a goofy grin. He directly engaged the audience at multiple points, both in person and through the livestream chat, and seemed like he was genuinely honored to be there. “To be up close and personal with y’all is special,” he said pensively. “It’s been a dream of mine to perform here.” Keeping with the low-key theme of the evening, the guests Bieber invited onstage mirrored his laid-back vibe. Rather bringing out big-ticket artists like previous collaborators Big Sean or SZA, Bieber kept it in the family, inviting SWAG architect Dijon to join him for “DEVOTION,” frequent collaborator and mentee the Kid Laroi for “STAY,” and virtuoso guitarist Mk.gee to close out “DAISIES.” He also returned the 2024 invite from Tems and Wizkid. There was something incredibly meta about seeing the biggest celebrity born from the golden age of YouTube run through the biggest hits of his career through AirPlay on a laptop. Rumors swirled earlier in the week that Justin had been sound-checking some of his older songs for Coachella, including generational classics like “Baby,” “Sorry,” and “Where Are Ü Now,” but no one knew the context. Turns out he just wanted to take a trip down memory lane, playing his music videos quite literally in real time on YouTube — at one point the video buffered, and he lamented about the shitty desert Wi-Fi. This section allowed him to toy with the audience’s excitement, asking if they were “really with the shits” before searching tracks like “Never Say Never,” “Confident,” and “Beauty and a Beat.” It was a welcome jolt of energy after the downtempo SWAG cuts, and it culminated in him playing the covers that got him discovered: Chris Brown’s “With You” and Ne-Yo’s “So Sick.” He even harmonized with his prepubescent self, riffing and hitting the same syncopation from two decades earlier. Justin clearly spent his time on iFunny back in the day. After speedrunning through some of his career-best hits, he arrived at the viral-video section of the show, taking the opportunity to play some classic YouTube videos of him running into a glass door and falling off the stage. It contributed to a slumber-party atmosphere, bringing the audience into an intimate living-room hang, as if we were all passing the laptop back and forth to show each other the videos we’ve seen a million times. He even jokingly recited the famous “It’s not clocking …” paparazzi video word for word as it played behind him. It was a remarkably self-reflexive move on one of the world’s biggest stages, and for someone who was clowned on in the media for nearly two decades, it was a privilege (and the best possible outcome) to watch him look back at himself and laugh. Without giving him too much credit, a deeper read of Bieberchella could land it somewhere close to performance art. Hear me out! In keeping it simple and reflecting on his old hits through the portal where he was discovered, the persona of Justin Bieber was reassessed and deconstructed in real time after years of mythos and controversy. He established what we remember him to be, placed it in the context of his newfound stripped-back image, and rebuilt himself from the ground up while acknowledging the fact he was doing it. To call his performance lacking in effort is a shallow read; Bieber spent the entirety of his set confronting the idea of both his own celebrity and the concept of digital fame as a whole, reflecting on his evolution as a heartthrob to millions of millennials, and, for a long time, the world’s punching bag. It’s a career-spanning victory lap and a big step forward in both artistic vision and the performance of self-mockery. As he told us back in 2010, “It’s always fun to make fun of yourself.” Everything That Happened During Bieberchella 2026 Your product is saved!
